text: Max Vuyisile Sisulu, born on 23 August 1945 in Soweto, is a South African politician and businessman who served as Speaker of the National Assembly from May 2009 to May 2014. A member of the African National Congress (ANC), he was part of the party's National Executive Committee (NEC) from December 1994 to December 2017. The son of anti-apartheid activists Albertina and Walter Sisulu, he is the eldest of five children, with siblings Mlungisi, Zwelakhe, Lindiwe, and Nonkululeko. In 1963, at age 19, he and his mother were arrested after his father went into hiding; his father was later sentenced to life imprisonment in the Rivonia Trial. After his release, Sisulu left South Africa for exile via Gaborone, Botswana, and moved to Tanzania, where he joined Umkhonto we Sizwe. Over the next decade, he lived in various regions of Africa and Europe, completing a master's degree in political economy from the Plekhanov Russian University of Economics in Moscow in 1969, a senior military training course in Skhodnya, Soviet Union in 1972, a one-year research fellowship at the University of Amsterdam in 1985, and serving as the ANC's representative in Budapest. From 1986 to 1990, he was head of the ANC's Department of Economic Planning at its headquarters in Lusaka, Zambia. In 1990, he returned to South Africa during the end of apartheid negotiations and became the founding director of the National Institute of Economic Policies in Johannesburg. In 1993, he earned a Master of Public Administration from the Harvard Kennedy School of Government. In April 1994, during South Africa's first democratic elections, Sisulu was elected to the National Assembly, the lower house of the new Parliament, and appointed as the inaugural chairperson of the Portfolio Committee on the Reconstruction and Development Programme (RDP), a policy he had helped draft. He was elected to the ANC NEC in 1994 and to the National Working Committee (NWC) in 1997. In February 1997, he became Chief Whip of the Majority Party, succeeding Arnold Stofile, and announced plans to restore the RDP committee's status and introduced academic training for MPs and staff. He resigned from Parliament in November 1998 to enter business, first joining Denel as deputy chief executive officer from 1998 to 2001, then becoming group general manager at Sasol from 2003 to 2006, and later holding various directorships, including at African Rainbow Minerals. He remained active in the ANC, being re-elected to the NEC and re-appointed to the NWC in December 2002 and December 2007, and served as chairperson of the NEC's Subcommittee on Economic Transformation until after the 53rd National Conference in December 2012, when Enoch Godongwana succeeded him. In the April 2009 general election, he returned to the National Assembly, ranked 39th on the ANC list, and was elected unopposed as Speaker on 6 May, replacing Gwen Mahlangu-Nkabinde, with Nomaindia Mfeketo as deputy. He was nominated by Andrew Mlangeni and was the first man to serve as Speaker since 1994 and the first black man ever to hold the position. He served throughout the Fourth Parliament, widely respected for his fairness and levity, and oversaw the establishment of the parliamentary budget office. During his tenure, he established an ad hoc parliamentary committee to examine the Public Protector's report on the Nkandla homestead upgrades, which found President Jacob Zuma had benefited unduly and should repay the state. Opposition parties welcomed his action, and he was later criticized by some within the ANC for initiating the committee, though the ANC denied such rebukes. The committee did not complete its work before the end of the parliamentary term. In the May 2014 general election, he was ranked 14th on the ANC list, but the party announced Baleka Mbete would replace him as Speaker, with observers suggesting this reflected a desire for stricter partisan control. Sisulu was sworn in as an ordinary MP on 21 May but resigned eight days later after failing to be appointed to President Zuma's cabinet, a move that surprised observers, though the ANC denied claims he was punished for the Nkandla investigation. After leaving Parliament, he remained active in the ANC, criticizing President Zuma in April 2016 following the Economic Freedom Fighters v Speaker judgment, calling for his resignation, and condemning Zuma's failure to support Finance Minister Pravin Gordhan as "bloody foolish," attending a civil society march in Pretoria in support of Gordhan. He served the remainder of his NEC term but was not re-elected at the December 2017 national conference. On 31 January 2018, he was appointed as an independent non-executive director of Harmony Gold. In 1966, he married Mercy Vutela, the daughter of activist Greta Ncapayi, whom he had known since high school; they reunited in exile in Moscow. Their son, Mlungisi, became a diplomat in South African embassies to Khartoum and Prague and died of cerebral malaria in London in January 2008 at age 40. His first marriage was short-lived. In 1979, he married Elinor Sisulu, a writer he met in Amsterdam in 1985, who later published a biography of her parents-in-law.
